Recent progress in Session-based Recommendation models has enabled the impressive result of generating recommendations directly as ranked lists. Although efficient for single-item lists, these models struggle to produce high-quality ranked lists containing multiple items. We introduce PRNE, a two-stage approach designed to create superior ranked lists of any length. The first stage employs an encoder to map session history and previous item recommendations into a compact candidate rank embedding. This embedding subsequently captures the performance potential of an item list, influencing how individual items within that stage are evaluated. The second stage utilizes this embedding in a regression task to predict scores for every possible item. We then apply a score normalization technique to transform these regression predictions into well-calibrated, ranked lists. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method consistently outperforms both traditional ranking- and session-based recommendation models.

We model an assembly of active colloids featuring two linked rods that navigate within an environment experiencing non-equilibrium strain. This system is governed by a shape parameter determining the distance and relative orientation between propulsion forces at each head. This relative propulsion generates effective interactions, transforming the colloids into active matter equivalents with properties resembling elastic springs. When placed in a strain field, these entities form dynamic networks capable of self-propulsion, functioning as autonomous agents within the simulation. This research concentrates on these colloidal structures within flow-induced strain fields that vary along their position. The study quantifies the response through the computation of an effective inertia tensor, which demonstrates that strong internal heads-to-head attraction fosters behaviors analogous to a mass-spring-mass model, complete with an effective mass subject to internal spring constants. Furthermore, this configuration exhibits directional swimming at low speeds and forms when the connection between the two units is tight. This research demonstrates that close coupling and active spring dynamics enable the dual-head molecule to exhibit persistent, self-directed motion.

We introduce a three-dimensional discrete fracture network model designed to simulate fluid transport and associated phenomena within discrete fracture network models. To address this, we develop a novel mesh generation strategy that creates a conforming multidimensional structure. This approach explicitly aligns with the codimension of various geometric elements, classifying them as either matrix blocks or fractures of codimension 0, co-dimension 1 (single or doubly connected 1D surfaces), or codimension-2 fractures within the 3D domain. For the mesh within each dimension, we employ concepts of discrete duality to define dual domains that conformally link primal elements. This foundation enables the application of mimetic finite difference techniques, yielding a high-order, property-preserving scheme that maintains conservation, discrete symmetry, and discrete adjointness. Furthermore, the scheme generalizes the concept of co-dimension-1 fluxes and operators, ensuring that the resulting mimetic discretization remains conservative and robust for all dimensions up to and including the co-dimension-2 fractures in the 3D domain. Numerical examples are provided to validate the accuracy and convergence of the proposed scheme.

This paper addresses collision avoidance and formation maintenance for multi-UAV systems through the centroid-based point-set registration framework. By defining a desired formation geometry scaled proportionally to the number of available drones, the method aligns actual formation centroids with those of this theoretical scaled template. An optimization-based optimization strategy determines the specific transformations applied to each drone, minimizing the least squares deviation between these point sets. This approach yields a unique solution that ensures a structured collision-free configuration. While effective for dynamic formation control, increasing flight distances between drones during dynamic scaling can amplify system dynamics under certain initial configurations. Consequently, the proposed solution was applied both in simulation environments and in real-world experiments with five quadcopters to validate its efficacy.
We examine the spectrum of the Seidel matrix in chain graphs. Specifically, we determine all eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix, identify its multiplicity, and calculate its distance between nodes.

This study investigates a mean-field optimal control framework where stochastic differential equations involve both delay and fractional Brownian motion driven by a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Since direct application of standard control techniques is hindered by the lack of the Markov property in these equations, the authors first establish the associated forward-backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) and subsequently derive the Hamiltonian along with the first-order necessary conditions for optimality expressed as forward-backward stochastic differential equilibrium equations. Distinct from prior research, the inclusion of fractional Brownian motion necessitates specific updates to both the Hamiltonian construction and the derivation of gradient formulas for the cost functional, updates that rely heavily on application of Clark-Sorner's rule and resolution of particular coupled partial differential integral equations. Finally, a numerical example is provided to support these findings.

This study introduces a novel architecture for road-side unit (RSU) and vehicle relay networks designed to boost vehicular ad hoc network (VANET) communication range and data throughput. The proposed framework consists of two hierarchical layers. In the first layer, an RSU functions as a gateway to connect with nearby vehicles within a specific area, facilitating seamless integration between vehicle networks and the Internet. The second layer comprises multiple vehicle relays that extend the RSU's coverage, improving both communication range and throughput. We constructed an analytical model for this system to determine key performance indicators, including transmission success probability, end-to-end delivery ratio, average latency, and system capacity. These averages were validated through numerical simulations. Furthermore, we analyzed how the densities of vehicles, RSUs, and relays impact overall network performance. The results indicate that increasing the density of vehicles and relays significantly enhances network transmission capacity while simultaneously reducing average latency.

Although Wikipedia serves as a primary source for encyclopedic content worldwide, it is often constrained by inherent limitations. Efforts to enhance its reliability rely on volunteers who possess domain expertise; however, such content created by unqualified individuals may introduce inaccuracies. Despite previous attempts to objectively detect articles lacking expertise, this effort remains insufficient. This paper introduces a novel methodology for identifying such substandard contributions by analyzing the characteristic editing patterns of anonymous users. By employing unsupervised learning to profile individual revisions, this approach enables the categorization of content quality without requiring an extensive labeled dataset. A significant advantage of this technique is its scalability, as it accommodates any number of new users or articles without necessitating system retraining. Furthermore, this system is fully adaptable and can be updated continuously as data expands. Our analysis of German Wikipedia data reveals that this methodology effectively Wahls out existing detection strategies.

Knowledge distillation serves as an effective strategy for accelerating deep learning inference, yet standard methods rely on access to a trained model's soft probabilities, rendering them ineffective when applied to decision-only black-box systems. This paper introduces a novel form of zero-shot knowledge distillation targeting decision-based black boxes. The approach relies on extracting patterns from the adversary's decisions by employing an evaluation model to infer hidden soft labels of the target. These soft labels enhance a teacher model which is then distilled into a faster student. The method was validated on image classification tasks using state-of-the-art adversaries such as Basic Forensics and Deep Forensics as the target, successfully demonstrating that accurate and efficient results can be achieved without any access to the adversary's internal code or probability outputs.

This report details the initial observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode and presents evidence for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$. The analysis utilizes a dataset corresponding to 3.8 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ is measured as $(1.84\pm0.34\pm0.24)\times10^{-3}$ relative to $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \pi^0$, with relative uncertainties derived from comparable measurements. Furthermore, the mass of the $B_s^0$ meson is determined through this process as $5.367\pm0.014$ (stat) $0.053$ (sys) GeV/$c^2$, a result that aligns well with previous determinations.

This paper demonstrates the application of B-fields on topological T-duality for twisted torus spaces, specifically showing how to classify such twisted tori spaces and compute the classification of principal $SO(n)$- and $GL(n, \mathbb{Z})$-B-fields within this context.

Imitation learning primarily enhances general reinforcement learning by utilizing expert demonstrations, but this approach often fails in practice due to limited availability of such experts. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework dubbed Co-Imitation Learning (CoCIL) that operates without requiring any prior expert knowledge. The methodology involves simultaneously training a policy encoder and a policy network through a mutual training dynamic. Specifically, this shared policy encoder is engineered to produce consistent embeddings for actions that yield analogous environmental outcomes, relying solely on the generated policy to learn from its own historical actions. Furthermore, the core neural network is educated via a composite reward structure derived from both an internal consistency measure and an exploration-driven mechanism. Evaluated across varied benchmarks for demon-stration-free reinforcement tasks, our method achieved results superior to current state-of-the-art approaches.

While traditional methods for extrinsic robot calibration often depend explicitly on impact markers, they can encounter obstacles such as dust accumulation or difficulty in placement. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a fully learning-centered framework that eliminates physical markers by leveraging data collected from sensors equipped with robot-depth cameras. First, we propose a multi-task learning approach relying on a single end-to-end encoder to simultaneously perform fault-tolerant in-hand object detection, depth-based object localization, and 3D reconstruction. Second, we develop a phase-based calibration pipeline that utilizes an efficient self-check process to filter out erroneous data during the accumulation phase. Furthermore, we demonstrate both the practicality and precision of our proposed system through various experiments, finding our method yields comparable accuracy to existing techniques.

We introduce a treatment interference framework wherein a unit's response relies exclusively on its treatment condition and the treatment status of other units within its K-neighborhood. While existing techniques for identifying interference rely on tailored randomized experiments and conditioning-based tests centered on specific units, we provide criteria for selecting appropriate units within our proposed framework. Through simulation analysis, we assess the performance of established methods for uncovering network interference. The results demonstrate that applying our guidelines for focal unit selection yields more powerful testing capabilities for detecting interference than traditional experimental approaches.

We investigate neutrino luminosities generated by self-annihilation within a dark matter candidate that couples to the Standard Model exclusively through a pseudoscalar mediator, focusing on environments like nucleon stars. We determine that once non-relativistic temperatures are reached, neutrino production predominantly stems from on-shell processes involving the creation and subsequent decay of this pseudoscalar. By applying an expansion valid in the limit of high-temperature and low-density regimes, we derive analytical expressions for the chemical potentials and the leading-order terms governing dark matter neutrino emissivity. We further establish the precise conditions under which this derived analytical framework remains reliable and compare our analytical outcomes with numerical simulations to determine their domain of consistency. Finally, we estimate the pseudoscalar-mediated dark matter relic density by linking our findings to constraints derived from neutrino emission rates in neutron stars.

The Kronecker-Rweyl theorem establishes that for any irrational number $\alpha$, the sequence $n\alpha$ (for $n \in \mathbb{N}$) exhibits equidistribution modulo 1. Building on this foundation, we introduce a generalized version of the Kronecker-Rweyl type theorem. Specifically, given an irrational $\alpha$ satisfying a specified Diophantine approximation condition, we demonstrate the equidistribution of the hybrid sequence $n\alpha + f(n)$ modulo 1, where $f(n)$ is a polynomial with rational coefficients. This result serves as a pivotal step toward proving our primary finding: a collection of equivalence theorems concerning the equidistribution modulo 1 of $n\alpha + f(n)$ under the stronger condition that $\alpha$ satisfies the stated Rweyl criterion for order $n$. These findings also yield significant applications in understanding joint distribution patterns of $n\alpha$ and $f(n)$.

The emergence of quantum spin systems within the class of solid-state materials enables groundbreaking research into how fundamental interactions among spins drive system-wide magnetic behaviors. Among these phenomena are ordered phases characterized by long-range magnetic order, as well as disordered phases appearing specifically in two-dimensional spin lattices, known as quantum spin liquids. Unlike ordered states, quantum spin liquids support non-ordered, entangled quantum magnetic order, which has recently been observed in the two-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet $\text{NiBr}_2$. This material offers a rare experimental model for studying the complex interplay between magnetic order and entanglement. In this study, we demonstrate that applying a uniaxial field along the $c$-axis in $\text{NiBr}_2$ allows for precise tuning between two distinct quantum spin liquid phases: the topological phase, linked to the anyonic Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless state, and the nodal phase, associated with gapless excitations. By analyzing interphase transitions, we have identified an emergent phase transition point, which, when combined with existing findings, establishes a complete three-phase field diagram. These findings provide critical experimental validation for theoretical models and significantly advance our understanding of quantum critical points in 2D Heisenberg antiferromagnets.

Pseudo-RNGs in SRAM-based SoCs are vulnerable to side-channel attacks because their output sequences are easily predictable. To defend against this, this paper proposes TuRaN, an SRAM-based True-RNG designed with a new methodology to ensure security even if partial output leakage occurs. The approach exploits intrinsic unpredictability in the power consumption of SRAMs, specifically targeting voltage fluctuations caused by concurrent operations. To extract random bits from this data, a two-stage filtering process employs lightweight cryptographic primitives. Furthermore, since RNGs must pass stringent statistical and cryptographic assessments, both principles and the generated sequences were rigorously evaluated. This paper details the full testing framework, including three information-theoretic scenarios covering both pre- and post-processing stages, as well as three statistical standard tests, all of which TuRAN successfully passed.

This study examines the internal structure of hybrid stars, which are supported against gravitational collapse by a combination of hadronic and quark degenerate pressures. In our approach, several HARPtonic pressure formulas are matched with the stress from quantum formulas of mass-energy. We look at three specific models that make up the star structure: two main models and one additional model. We also examine how these stars behave when they cross over from hadronic matter to quark degenerate pressure sources using two different theoretical frameworks for converting mass into quark pressure sources. By varying parameters related to quark pressure sources and matching them with gravitational effects, we look at how these stars change their size and stability as their core composition changes from hadronic to quark degenerate pressure sources. We also examine how these changes in size and stability are related to the transition in mass-energy between the two different pressure sources. Finally, we discuss how these findings can help us understand the internal structure of hybrid stars and how they relate to other sources of gravitational wave emission.

An optomechanical setup involving three-level atomic transitions and subject to the q-deformation parameter is investigated. Using the formalism of input-output relations alongside a Hermitian Adams-Loucks approach for computing scattering and transmission matrices, the authors analyze photon transport characteristics within the device. Findings from a numerical analysis of the transmission spectra are used to support the proposed theoretical framework. These results validate the accuracy of the theory by demonstrating physical effects such as transparency windows, as well as significant peaks and valleys in the transmission spectrum. Additionally, the study identifies regions of both rapid and delayed photon propagation, observing both fast and slow light enhancements. Ultimately, it is concluded that adjusting the degree of q-deformation yields better control over photon transport phenomena within the system.

Recent advances in growing complex oxides as ultra-thin films have enabled the zoology approach to fluctuations—encompassing magnetic, electronic, structural, and stoichiometric variations—to be mapped across their intrinsic bulk phases and these extrinsic heterointerfaces. While some instabilities persist in both contexts others exist solely at films surfaces or interfaces. This review examines these phenomena specifically regarding local magnetic electronic structural and compositional fluctuations while emphasizing the distinct roles of strain and electronic mismatches in triggering them. We argue that these fluctuations may serve as vital precursors to emergent functional states such as superconductivity offering novel pathways for engineering new properties through engineered interfaces and controlled nano-structuring.

This study investigates how cryptocurrencies interact by analyzing individual trading volumes. Voluntary transactions are mapped into a network, where nodes represent specific coins and connecting lines reflect the trading relationships between them. Our analysis reveals an effective degree of nodes averaging around 5, suggesting transactions behave almost randomly at a fundamental level. Nevertheless, the research identifies similar patterns at the micro and mesoscopic scales repeatedly. Furthermore, the study examines the volatility of individual coins within these network contexts, uncovering distinct small-world characteristics. Using Maximum Entropy modeling, two approaches were applied: the traditional pairwise Ising model and a high-order extension incorporating three-way interactions. The traditional pairwise Ising model proved inadequate at capturing real-world data dynamics. Conversely, the three-way interaction model significantly outperformed pairwise methods, offering a more precise mathematical description. This success implies that high-order interactions play a critical role in cryptocurrency market dynamics. Ultimately, the findings suggest that simple two-variable representations are insufficient, and understanding the market requires acknowledging the collective influence of groups of assets acting together.

Forming new aerosols from existing ones is a critical prerequisite for cloud formation in the clear, lower atmosphere. This nucleation event relies on clusters of sulfuric acid and water molecules, where water molecules vibrate significantly. These must be modeled using quantum mechanical QM-QM methods that incorporate molecule-specific force fields to simulate these vibrations via quasi-adiabatic approximation. These quasi-adiabatic approaches allow the significance of zero-point energy within nucleating clusters to be assessed. We have applied this method to recent small clusters, specifically H₂O₆[(H₂SO₄)H₂O]ₙ for n = 0, 1, and 10. The findings indicate that while the role of zero-point energy grows as cluster size increases, its impact on cluster stability remains minor for these specific systems.

We introduce the concept of a perception pair $(X,A;\phi,\psi)$, consisting of a compact convex set along with two functions linking it to another convex set, where both preserve midpoints. We demonstrate that midpoints must be uniquely determined and establish a compactification for the space of all such operators. Furthermore, we examine group equivariant non-expansive operators. Using our techniques, we provide an alternative proof of Dufourrout's theorem regarding equivariant COB representations for $\mathbb{Z}_2$-equivariant maps defined on the disc with its boundary. Additionally, we extend Dufourrout's result to higher-dimensional equivariance structures.

The connection between dissipative transport and Hall responses in solids has been examined through various analogies to fluid dynamics. The "generalized gravitational analogy" postulates that a velocity field drives diffusing excitations, while the Einstein relations describe fluctuations related to this motion's kinetic energy. In this study, we demonstrate that both concepts fail when applied to diffusing anyons within hyperbolic superconductors. Although the analogies hold well for longitudinal responses, they break down transversely due to distinct transformation rules for gradients versus those required for Jacobians under coordinate changes. Furthermore, the fluctuation amplitudes predicted by the Einstein relations fail to match those observed in thermal diffusive Hall conductivity. These predictions indicate transverse momentum correlations arising from momentum-space vorticity that scale with the square root of the bulk dissipation rather than the bulk itself.

Simpler models are often favored over more complex ones, with this preference commonly enforced via explicit regularization. However, many unsupervised learning tasks inherently possess implicit complexity controls that can benefit supervised models. This paper introduces methods to quantify various aspects of model complexity, particularly geometric features such as the number of neurons activated. Using these metrics as surrogates for complex counts, we observe that explicit regularization measures align closely with these geometric metrics at low loss levels. Consequently, unsurprising simple solutions emerge in the absence of explicit penalties simply because the model's inherent geometry limits further loss reduction. Engineers have long envisioned creating robotic systems capable of identifying other moving objects within a video stream to track them or initiate interactions. The system leverages the distinctive oscillation inherent in biological movements and the inherent instability of biological organisms under gravity. Recent advancements in conditionally guided audio synthesis, specifically those leveraging images for visual support, have yielded impressive results. However, these models often struggle with producing diverse or high-fidelity outputs that depend on minor visual variations, such as slight changes in an object's orientation. This lack of control from the visual condition is particularly problematic for applications like synthetic data creation. Although increasing training data diversity usually enhances generator output variety, the existing models fail to generalize effectively to new images, yielding repetitive audio even when exposed to diverse training images. We identify the core issue as a lack of distinct visual-audio associations in latent space, where similar inputs fail to produce varied outputs because the training process collapses similar conditions into uniform acoustic results. To resolve this, we propose V-GAN, a framework that utilizes a disentanglement prior to create semantically separate latent factors: one branch dissects the input image while the other processes audio. By applying disentanglement constraints to both visual and acoustic latent spaces, we establish clear correspondences between specific latent codes and their features. This structured mapping enables audio generation that is precisely controlled by visual inputs, including the synthesis of conditionally aligned sequences that exhibit significant stylistic diversity. Extensive experiments confirm our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in generating controlled and varied content, while also supporting a new application: the interpolation of both audio and joint image-sound pairs directly from the generated latent mappings.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are well established for modeling sequential data, yet recent research indicates that deep learning approaches which update weights after every single data step (recurrence) fail to outperform non-recurrent baselines that process data in batches. Moreover, analysis reveals that RNNs equipped with learned schedules for batch updates more efficiently represent data compared to those updating at every step or models lacking recurrent connections entirely.

In an era where information spreads rapidly, the proliferation of misinformation poses significant risks, particularly concerning the adoption or refusal of COVID-19 vaccines. Sintered samples of these extraterrestrial materials were created using a high-voltage plasma-arc source and evaluated through point hardness, flexural strength, and bending tests, while post-sintering microstructures were analyzed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and point SEM. Sintering conditions significantly altered microstructure, resulting in the formation of glassy bonds and glassy bonds contained within particle interfaces contained the formation of glassy bonds. Notably, an optimal temperature of 800°C produced superior outcomes for both lunar and lunar materials, yielding the highest mechanical properties. While mechanical performance was generally superior for sintered lunar regolith, Martian materials demonstrated notable improvements across all temperatures. These findings indicate that the temperature-dependent microstructure changes are a primary driver of enhanced mechanical behavior, suggesting that thermal processing offers a viable method for strengthening and reinforcing potential regolith-based construction materials used for in situ resource utilization on the Moon and Mars.

Occupancy modeling is a standard method for evaluating the presence or absence of a species while accounting for the uncertainty inherent in detection processes. This approach is applicable across diverse habitats, from terrestrial environments to those ranging from shorelines out to the open ocean. Over recent decades, researchers have expanded these methods to accommodate spatial data through spatial occupancy models and to incorporate information from multiple spatially coherent traps. Furthermore, these extensions have evolved to weigh results within a hierarchical framework, utilizing information from neighboring traps, and to integrate complementary data sources through integrated spatial occupancy models. The `spOccupancy` R package was created to facilitate the analysis of such complex multi- and spatially structured datasets. It enables fitting seven distinct models: spatial occupancy models, spatially coherent occupancy models, spatially coherent multi-species models, spatially coherent spatial occupancy models, as well as the latter two applied within an integrated framework. These models can be estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo for Bayesian approaches or via maximum likelihood estimation.

Laboratory experiments investigated the entrainment of the ambient fluid by an axisymmetric turbulent plume loaded with settling particles, where plume strength and particle properties such as size and density ratio were controlled as variables. Observations indicated particle-laden plumes have smaller radial velocity and momentum deficits than clean plumes under matching conditions, leading to reduced rise heights. Additionally, the radial velocity profile of the particle-laden jet broadens, resulting in particle-laden plumes that are more "turbulent" and penetrate deeper than their non-turbulent counterparts, despite the previously mentioned lower buoyancy flux. This increased turbulence is linked to particle-induced fluctuations that enhance vertical velocity variance, promoting greater entrainment relative to the pure jet. Consequently, the data reveal particle-laden plumes are less efficient at entraining the surrounding fluid; the entrainment coefficient decreases as buoyancy and particle parameters change, ultimately allowing higher particle concentrations to suppress the rise height entirely, causing the flow to behave more like a jet than a plume.

The spread of infectious agents through populations is frequently modeled by adapting the classic SIR (susceptible, infectious, recovered) epidemiological framework. While traditional applications of this model rely on pairwise contact networks represented by graphs, a growing number of interactions occur simultaneously within social cliques, professional teams, or online groups. To address this, researchers have recently generalized the SIR system to hypergraphs, which utilize multi-way interactions rather than simple edges. In this paper, we establish the spectral threshold conditions governing the survival of an epidemic within a general population structure composed of hypergraphs. Our findings demonstrate that basic reproductive numbers in this context correspond to principles of large deviations, specifically the action of a quasi-free measure. Additionally, we derive a sufficient criterion ensuring almost certain disease extinction and provide a detailed analysis of the distribution of infected durations. In the final section, we apply our theoretical results to a concrete scenario featuring triangular contact patterns.

We present first-principles-based spin-textural calculations for CrI₃, a two-dimensional ferromagnetic insulator, which exhibits magnetic ordering along the out-of-plane direction. Our results reveal that the spin moments are concentrated on the atomic columns, and the spin textures of the valence and conduction bands are nearly identical. However, a slight disparity in these textures, along with the absence of spin moment splitting, is attributed to the finite value of the Berry curvature dipole, which originates from structural centrosymmetry in the lattice. Additionally, we identify that the ferromagnetic state breaks magnetic point group symmetry, enabling the emergence of a Chern moment that governs the spin polarization observed at the material's edges. Ultimately, our findings suggest that spin textures in 2D ferromagnetic insulators are sensitive to both the Berry curvature curvature dipole and the Rashba-like effect induced by the edge Chern moment.

Observations indicate that as solar-like stars reduce their rotation rates, the amplitude of their magnetic cycles diminishes, eventually disappearing in systems rotating significantly slower than the Sun's. Theoretical models struggle to replicate this trend, often predicting enhanced magnetic activity under slower rotation conditions. We propose that this discrepancy arises from a link between rotation speed and the emergence zone's latitude, where slower rotators exhibit dynamos operating in higher latitudes. Consequently, differential rotation is weaker in these cases, resulting in less efficient magnetic churning and a lack of magnetic cycle behavior. To address this, we incorporated the anti-solar rotation profile, characterized by faster equatorial and slower polar rotation, observed in spot-active giants, alongside an elevated emergence zone into our magnetohydrodynamic simulations. We argue that dynamos function similarly in these higher-latitude emergence regions, with differential rotation governed by a law inversely proportional to latitude. By adjusting theoretical findings, we argue that differential rotation in such regions is inherently modest, offering a new perspective on why magnetic cycles may halt in slowly rotating stars.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) excel in various computer vision and pattern recognition domains, prompting extensive research into multi-object detection, multi-image classification, and multi-label prediction. However, these tasks often lack single unified detection frameworks. This paper introduces a novel Generalized K-fan Multimodal Deep Model (GKFMDM), designed to address several multi-object prediction challenges by integrating DNNs with shared representations. This architectural approach induces a linear dependency relationship among network outputs, enabling inputs to generate correlated responses that align with distinct but related tasks. We establish the theoretical framework for the proposed model, derive its optimal parameters using Bregman divergences to enhance learning, and achieve optimal Bregman divergence through an optimized output layer activation function. Additionally, the work demonstrates applications of the new architecture on multi-image classification and multi-object detection. Experimental results across multi-image classification on ImageNet and multi-object detection on the PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset confirm the model's significant potential.

Model checking serves as a prominent formal method for verifying program correctness, yet existing implementations typically struggle with scalability when analyzing large codebases due to excessive state explosion caused by multithreading ambiguities. To address this, we introduce McMini, a model checker that enhances scalability by integrating minimal context DPOR (Directional Overlapping Preorder Handling). Our implementation features several critical contributions: first, a generalization of minimal context DPOR applicable to algorithm variations; second, the adaptation of this approach to Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT)-backed schedulers; third, the integration of back translation techniques to further reduce state explosion. Our results demonstrate that McMini successfully scales to verify industrial-sized applications and prior test suites that existing DPOR-based tool could not verify previously.

WhatsApp currently holds the distinction of being the most widespread messaging application globally, boasting 2 billion registered users. Its popularity is largely driven by exceptional privacy safeguards, including robust encryption, coupled with versatility in reaching both individuals and groups. Unfortunately, this emphasis on privacy has inadvertently facilitated the rapid dissemination of disinformation, a problem that severely impacts the integrity of elections. Recently, numerous nations, particularly in South Asia and Latin America, have turned to imposing technical constraints on message forwarding within the app as a countermeasure against rumors. However, virtually no scholarly research exists regarding how such limitations effectively combat disinformation. Consequently, our ethnographic fieldwork conducted in the Philippines provides fresh empirical insights into users' responses when WhatsApp rumors spread during a national voting cycle. Our findings suggest that while message forwarding restrictions may diminish the overall reach of unverified information, they often have unintended consequences, such as enhancing rumor credibility or driving them toward alternative communication channels. Ultimately, our study offers nuanced perspectives on limiting information flow via super-apps and highlights critical avenues for further investigation into digital disinformation mitigation.

The paper proposes $\Lambda$-like coalescent approximations for a broad class of supercritical branching processes. We focus on the frequency spectrum of these supercritical types, where individuals within an allele share a common ancestor at a specific time. Our findings demonstrate that, provided the branching process possesses a finite logarithmic moment and the associated $\Lambda$-coalescent is absolutely continuous, acceptable coalescent approximations exist in the high-asymptotic limit of population growth. We explicitly characterize the necessary conditions for the frequency functions of both the high- and low-frequency categories for both supercritical branching processes and their corresponding $\Lambda$-coalescents. Furthermore, we establish that effective historical population size increases linearly with generations as a function of time, while relative effective population sizes scale based on a power law determined by the growth rate exponent, particularly for critical populations near extinction or expansion thresholds.

The primary objective of spoofing detection systems is to identify synthetic artifacts embedded in speech resulting from synthesis or conversion processes. This study introduces the incorporation of attention mechanisms directly into the activation functions of the deep learning architectures used for detection. This novel approach, which we name the Attentive Activation Function (AAF), offers a fully differentiable solution that is simpler and less resource-intensive than embedding attention within the network's structural layers. Focusing on neural networks that map raw audio feature sequences of length $L$ to a single spoofing probability score, we evaluate the method by comparing standard activation functions with the proposed AAF-Arfnn model. Experiments demonstrate that integrating this function yields improvements, particularly in models that compress the length $L$ using pooling or bottleneck mechanisms. Additionally, we provide an analytical explanation for these observations and establish benchmarks for future comparison.

"An analysis of locally supersymmetric effective field theories (EFTs) governing the inflaton examines how supersymmetry constrains inflaton dynamics and identifies new physical effects when supersymmetry is treated as "soft." Building on a previous study that developed the supersymmetry-breaking EFT for a minimally supersymmetric model, this work extends that framework to compute inflaton two-point and three-point correlation functions explicitly at one-loop order. These computations involve integrating over the inflaton power spectrum to determine the inflaton's three-loop correction and investigating the influence of supersymmetry violations on inflaton interactions."

Nonreciprocal optical systems, which replicate parallel circuits operating in reverse directions, have garnered significant interest for developing advanced non-reciprocal components such as circulators and directional switches. This research demonstrates a fundamentally distinct form of nonreciprocity appearing in the correlation statistics of photon pairs generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing. While standard single-particle optical nonreciprocity arises from differences in linear dispersion or particle presence between forward and reverse paths, this new phenomenon originates for two particles from a discrepancy in dispersion relations for forward and reverse propagation. Nonreciprocal behavior in photon pair correlations cannot be accounted for by conventional approaches like magnetic induction or circulating optical孤波; instead, it requires components with inherently directionally dependent dispersion characteristics. Crucially, unlike single-particle effects, this nonreciprocity in twin photon pairs persists even when both propagation directions share identical dispersion profiles. We propose that realizing this phenomenon relies on utilizing nonlinear optics with a spatially asymmetric geometry, specifically citing examples such as photonic crystals and nonlinear microresonators.

Superconducting quantum circuits are recognized as a promising platform for realizing quantum computation and simulation. However, comprehending their quantum behavior demands sophisticated theoretical models that can be validated with exceptional theoretical accuracy. By employing near-field terahertz scanning microscopy, we demonstrate precise mapping of nanoscale near-field electromagnetic distributions within superconductors adjacent to planar resonators. Our findings confirm deep penetration of terahertz penetrates into the superconducting material, yielding significantly nonlocal boundary conditions that substantially improve the accuracy of circuit models compared to the traditional perfect-conductor approximation. Additionally, we demonstrated that scanning probe measurements can detect superconducting transitions, thereby validating the capability to observe phase transitions in superconducting quantum circuitry.

Financial markets are constantly shifting due to the collective actions of various market participants. To better understand these complex interactions, particularly how they drive price movements, researchers increasingly rely on agent-based models. Previously, we explored these models further by examining agents' reactions to historical data, specifically whether agents new to the system profit from strategies that worked for experienced agents in past market data. This paper investigates the broader question of return spillover from established strategies to the entries of new agents following these agents' entries. The study reveals that existing strategies generate significant spillover effects for new agents in both traditional price data and alternative data types, demonstrating that an agents' reactions to historical data strongly predict their future success both individually and collectively. This finding indicates that effective agents adapt their behaviors based on collective historical patterns, a critical insight for enhancing both financial modeling and predictive forecasting.

Protocol detection involves the critical network security task of identifying the application layer protocol to enable proper packet classification. Because current open-source NIDS rely heavily on this function to maintain operational efficacy, protocol detection represents a pivotal control mechanism whose failure can compromise system functionality. This paper demonstrates the ability to evade the dynamic protocol identification used by popular NIDS—specifically Snort, OSSEC, and Suricata—by introducing variations of just four bytes within the protocol payload. These modifications are sufficient to trigger classification mismatches, resulting in analysis errors. Given the severity of such mismatches, understanding these vulnerabilities is essential for developing more robust packet classifiers and protocols with enhanced resilience to detection bypass attacks.

Electrical circuits that integrate superconductors and semiconductors utilize Josephson junctions as tunable switches to manage power consumption. This study reveals a surprising capability to also control magnons (spin waves) in adjacent magnetic ferrimagnetic yttriumIG, a material selected for its thin-film compatibility and stable magnon properties. By modulating the junction's critical current, we demonstrate active on/off switching of magnons with greater than 99% efficiency and switchable gains exceeding 3 dB. This effect stems from the precession of magnetization within the magnetic layer, amplified by an effective field modulation produced at the interface with the superconductor—achieved through two key mechanisms: the proximity effect and the Meissner effect. These findings highlight a critical advancement, proving that active magnon gating is no longer theoretical and enabling new superconductive-magnetic architectures for both quantum information processing and classical computing.

Federated learning with novel classes presents significant hurdles, particularly when categories are absent from local datasets during training. Additionally, introducing entirely new classes later on in the model's lifecycle presents further difficulties. To address these issues, we propose an architecture optimized for scenarios where clients lack data for old as well as newly introduced classes. Demonstrated through a pixel-based intro, the system shows improved handling of unknown categories compared to baseline methods. Nevertheless, the approach sacrifices some accuracy regarding entirely new classes relative to alternative solutions. The project's source codes are available at: https://github.com/Deeplearning-DLAB-IITJ/ZSFL

This Letter introduces a theoretical framework designed for comprehensive optical analysis of high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeinberger (GHZ) resources. The study initially validates this methodology through complete measurements of distinct three-photon GHZ states within a tripartite quantum basis. The approach is subsequently extended to generalize for entire photonic high-dimensional GHZ configurations. The utility of this proposed technique will ultimately serve photonic quantum computing applications by enabling comprehensive analysis of these substantial high-dimensional entangled resources involving photons.

This study investigates a channel estimation method for intelligent surface (IS)-aided multi-user multiple-input multiple-output systems, utilizing cascaded channel models to mitigate IS component count during estimation while maintaining performance equivalent to standard models. The approach establishes an optimization framework for phase shift optimization that maximizes estimation performance. The analysis demonstrates that increasing the density of metasurface components toward the radio frequency signal source yields superior estimation results, particularly under low reflection scenarios, whereas performance remains consistent regardless of spatial distribution when the IS cluster remains large. The findings also reveal an inverse relationship between user proximity to the IS and estimation accuracy near the base station; closer proximity yields higher error rates due to a larger effective channel dimensionality requiring more coefficients, whereas distant users benefit from significant path loss attenuating weak non-cascaded paths, reducing their channel complexity and estimation errors. The proposed algorithm, which maximizes the minimum signal-to-error ratio (min MSEE), ensures balanced performance across all users. Finally, numerical evaluations confirm that the proposed channel estimation methodology significantly outperforms conventional IS-based techniques.

We analyze relationships between local news coverage and COVID-19 outcomes (cases and deaths), as well as audience metrics, using scIA, an automated content analysis system. Our findings show a positive link between news coverage and reported cases, but no correlation with mortality rates; this suggests media focus correlates with case activity rather than outcomes. We observe similar patterns for news and sales, indicating a rise in product purchases during surges in COVID cases. These results have significant implications for both scholars and practitioners.

Counting is an essential ability, yet its evolutionary emergence and historical introduction to human populations remain unexplained. We introduced a study designed to simulate this ability's origins by applying machine learning techniques to a primate-like population. These agents underwent iterative training on an artificial "pushing" task involving ordered beads, where the goal alternated between retrieving specific counts (e.g., the 2nd or last/1st in this context: 1st) based on visual input, with capabilities limited strictly to their immediate prior performance. Over successive generations, primates demonstrated a significant increase in task proficiency, culminating in the spontaneous emergence of robust primacy principles capable of accurately locating targets such as the 1st, 2nd, nth, 5th, 10th without explicit retraining. This primacy-based solution relied on the integration of two fundamental cognitive functions: (a) memory for accumulated sequence experiences and (b) the ability to retain relative positional labels (e.g., using terms like "firstly," "secondly," etc.). Crucially, this ability to locate nth items did not arise from explicit teaching, as these specific limitations were never part of the original task parameters. Instead, such teaching arose through the cumulative inheritance of knowledge across generations. These findings suggest that dominant cognitive strategies for handling novel tasks can be established through cultural transmission in non-human species, providing insights into how higher-order thinking evolves and spreads beyond initial discovery points.

Bloom filters solve the problem of rapidly determining set membership with a space complexity of $O(n/\epsilon)$ for a given failure probability $\delta$ and speed proportional to $O(1/\delta)$; these limits are theoretically optimal. Cuckoo filters improve upon Bloom filters by eliminating this time complexity penalty while maintaining the same space efficiency. However, both strategies struggle when dealing with data collections that are smaller than their respective optimal sizes. Introducing the xor filter overcomes these limitations for scenarios involving both very small collections and low failure rates.

Key topics include exploring the relationship between the L\^e--Yau center and the Duane center of a given log Enriques point, as well as examining centers related to various types of log polar spaces. We further analyze and provide new examples demonstrating that, for various classes of such spaces, the Duane, L\^e--Yau, and various other definitions of centers associated to a log polar space can all coincide. Several other results in these notes address relations among different kinds of log polar spaces as defined by various authors, with an emphasis on characteristics within Fano varieties and associated properties.

This research introduces a new market information framework based on the temporal sequence of transactions defined by time ($t$), price ($p$), and volume ($q$). We propose an information theoretic approach to quantify the predictive value of any specific order on future market movement. To model the optimal structure, we first establish a framework for ideal information that accounts for supply dynamics, demand pressure, and transaction volumes. Subsequently, we derive equations for both optimal and actual market paths using the provided order structure, enabling calculation of the predictive predictiveness of individual transactions. Finally, we validate our methodology by backtesting on historical ONEXS data to demonstrate its reliability.

This study introduces FLVoogd, a privacy-preserving federated learning framework designed to mitigate communication risks while preserving data confidentiality. In this approach, participants share model updates rather than training data, creating an environment where users, servers, and clients act non-collusively and encrypted interactions between clients and the server are maintained. To counter issues arising from non-independent and identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) data distributions, FLVoogd integrates a confidence-based resampling technique with the K-Means algorithm on the server side. Comprehensive experiments across four datasets—MNIST, FashionMNIST, Cifar10, and STL-10demonstrated that the proposed method significantly minimizes communication hazards and enhances accuracy and robustness. Compared to existing federated learning methods, FLVoogd achieves approximately a 42% reduction in total update transmission, simultaneously reducing computational overhead by 40% for data sampling and by 28% for general processing efficiency.

Deep learning models trained on synthetic data often struggle with real-world deployments due to the \textit{Sim2Real} gap. While data augmentation has shown some success, its capacity to fully close this gap remains limited. We introduce \textit{GradAlign}, a novel augmentation technique that remains agnostic to specific model architectures or training objectives. Instead, it matches gradient structures within loss functions by first synthesizing training images based on random transformations and subsequently mirroring the loss gradients of original inputs to these augmented counterparts. Our approach is integrated into a generative model producing realistic driving scenes to bridge the sim2real divide. Implemented using the connected driving framework and extending the popular OFFROAD and Cityscapes datasets, our method successfully reduces the sim2real gap with substantial gains.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have enabled创造出 highly realistic synthetic faces and voices, fueling malicious uses such as counterfeit news, deceptive social media, and identity fraud. While Detection DeepRecognition D is a proposed solution to mitigate these threats by identifying traces within synthetic content, most current approaches fail against fake samples drawn from domains outside their training sets—a well-known over-fitting issue that hampers generalizability. Consequently, there remains considerable challenge in developing robust detection robust against these limitations on unrestricted media. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the entire deepfake ecosystem, specifically generation and mechanisms. Moreover, our emphasis lies on methodologies for identifying synthetic faces and voices, particularly those designed for cross-domain adaptation. Finally, several critical open questions are proposed to guide future investigations in this field.

Recent findings indicate that sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets possessing H/He-dominated atmospheres below the equilibrium vapor pressure of silicate rock are likely widespread. For these "ocean worlds," surface materials dissolve into the atmosphere, creating blanketing clouds that can completely obscure the underlying ocean from observation. Nevertheless, within this specific regime, shrouded seas might still be detectable via distinct signatures in their transit profiles. A key differentiator between the effects of solubility-driven chemistry and thermochemistry is the non-monotonic variation of cloud particle radius with temperature for the latter; whereas particle size remains constant relative to temperature due purely on thermodynamic reasons. Consequently, solubility equilibrium produces unique spectral features during the different phases of a planet's orbit, generating detectable variations in the measured duration of the full transit. A similar differentiating mechanism applies to effective atmospheric scale heights: while these are governed solely by composition under solubility-driven conditions, they rely entirely on temperature under standard thermochemical rules. These specific "solubility equilibrium" regimes may prevail in planets with surface pressures below roughly 100 bar, potentially extending up to 1,000 bar. Detecting these unique solubility-dependent effects would provide definitive proof distinguishing planetary solubility equilibria from typical thermochemical atmospheric behavior.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), which utilize discrete spikes as a communication framework, represent the most basic form of sequential processing in artificial systems, yet current models struggle with limited temporal resolution and inefficient spike usage. Drawing inspiration from biological mechanisms, we introduce two improvements for enhancing sequence efficiency in SNNs under constrained time windows. First, by adopting the short-term synaptic potentiation found in neuroscience, our proposed Short-Term Memory (STM) synapse rules amplify short temporal connections to accelerate pre-spike signal transmission speed. Second, we implemented an Adaptive Integrate-and-Fire (ADIF) neuron model based on adaptive ion conductances observed in neuroscience; this model exhibits intrinsic firing patterns that reduce unnecessary spiking activity. Together, these mechanisms boost computational throughput and information density within Severe environments.

This paper introduces the Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) Challenge report, which analyzes the distinct difficulties associated with the OOU metric—specifically its focus on absolute OOU rate—and evaluates the current state of the art in addressing these complexities. Since the primary challenge lies in handling OOU data, which by definition involves unknown vocabulary, the needed strategies are inherently difficult to generalize. While many NLP tasks typically employ large-scale pre-training to overcome data scarcity, this approach risks compromising the OOU metric's accuracy due to the inherent limitation of never encountering the OOU data during both pre-training and fine-tuning phases. Although recent efforts have attempted to mitigate this gap, the core problem remains unsolved: fully mastering the capabilities of pre-training for both data generation and filtering without exposure to the target out-of-sample vocabulary. Given these constraints, our analysis reveals that current methods struggle to reliably capture OOU phenomena. These findings underscore critical, underexplored research directions, including the necessity of incorporating data from multiple domains and the development of vocabulary-specific representations. Representation learning that explicitly encodes vowel and consonant structures offers a promising avenue for creating more robust models capable of handling unseen linguistic variations.

The paper proposes a fully non-intrusive, data-driven framework for uncertainty propagation using generalized polynomial chaos (gPC) expansion, alongside several methods to assess A) the sufficiency of gPC convergence and B) the accuracy of statistical inferences drawn from gPC models. The first set ensures sufficient sample sizes for model training and reliable estimation of global sensitivity indices. The second ensures samples are adequate for estimating specific statistics of interest. The framework is evaluated using both synthetic and practical cases, specifically the uncertainty analysis of an airfoil and a pin fin heat transfer model.

The need to monitor industrial systems is a critical challenge in condition-based maintenance, a task complicated by the fact that condition indicators are often partially obscured by noise and unmodeled effects. This paper introduces a new approach for monitoring such systems by formulating it as a problem of sequentially detecting and isolating changes in a Markov model where the state is only partially observable. The proposed algorithm employs a grid-based technique to represent possible system states, which significantly lowers computational demands compared to traditional algorithms like the particle filter.

We investigate the stellar populations of 12 dwarf galaxies situated in the Local Volume, analyzing photometric and spectroscopic data to determine their star formation histories (SFHs) and in-situ stellar chemical abundances. By applying two-component modeling, we identify that 10 of the 12 dwarfs exhibit significant accretion events; these events typically began between 1.5 and 2.5 billion years ago, contributing roughly 10–40% of each galaxy's total stellar mass. Although some of these accretions likely involved rich accreted substructures, we find no evidence for dry accretion events that suppressed star formation. Consequently, the timing and cessation of star formation appear governed by internal mechanisms or external quenching methods other than dry accretion. Comparing our derived abundances with those predicted by $\Lambda$CDM simulations for in-situ populations reveals significant discrepancies, suggesting that much of the observable chemical diversity in dwarf galaxies originates from material inherited from accreted satellites.

Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is essential for the broader goal of developing generalizable visual language foundations. Because large visual requirements are met primarily through data labeling, the associated costs are substantial and prohibitive. To address this, we introduce a cost-constrained approach that introduces three core components: first, a selection mechanism to identify training samples with maximum diversity while maintaining steady model performance; second, a weak-annotation technique capable of applying basic information to roughly 95% of necessary training sets; third, two distinct weak-to-strong annotation strategies that fill remaining labeling gaps. Extensive experiments validating our approach across various diverse real-world document types demonstrate that our methods achieve comparable performance to baseline conven-tional sampling while achieving dramatic reductions in annotation expenses.

The magnetic properties of the Indium Antimonide (InAs) semiconducting substrate profoundly impact EuS metamaterials, yet electronic structure studies of the EuS/InAs interface remain scarce. Using density functional theory, this work examines how varying the orientation of Europium atoms relative to the InAs substrate orientation modifies the electronic properties of the interface. Findings reveal that regardless of orientation, a narrow band located at the $\bar{\Gamma}$ point within the bandgap exhibits strong hybridization between Eu $f/f$ and In $p$ orbitals. Notably, when Eu is oriented along the [110] direction, a significant number of Eu $f/f$ states shift outside the gap. These results provide crucial insights for designing interfaces in spin heterostructures involving EuS and InAs.

Data collection and annotation constitute expensive bottlenecks in deep learning model development. While self-training offers a solution by leveraging unlabeled data through pseudo-label generation, it typically suffers from accuracy and training instability, often necessitating manual intervention. Existing research generally addresses these issues by restricting their scope to small datasets or by applying this method only to initial model warm-up phases rather than throughout end-to-end training—a limitation stemming from the high computational cost of backpropagation on massive datasets combined with the infeasibility of restarting trained models from scratch. To overcome these constraints, this paper introduces **ClickTrain**, a novel fine-grained, architecture-preserving pruning technique for self-training. By performing backpropagation on pruned subsets during end-to-end training on full data, ClickTrain generates higher-quality labeled datasets of synthetic information. This approach yields significant benefits: it generates more effective training samples that improve both instability and accuracy, thereby reducing the volume of labeled data required, and it facilitates the efficient reuse of pretrained models. Experiments across three computer vision benchmarks, including the challenging COCO instance segmentation task, validate ClickTrain. Results demonstrate that the method consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches and achieves near-GPU-efficient scaling.

Markov Decision Processes represent a foundational model widely applied in fields like operations management and machine learning, typically aiming for an optimal policy that maximizes long-term discounted rewards. This paper introduces a novel primal-dual algorithm for addressing Constrained Markov Processes, achieving linear convergence rates from arbitrary starting points for both finite and countable Markov systems. The approach reformulates the problem as a linear programming task within a high-dimensional space and develops a primal-dual method specifically designed to solve this formulation efficiently. Additionally, the study establishes both the existence and constructive proofs for dual variables, ensuring feasible solutions. These findings demonstrate that practical, policy-feasible solutions emerge along the algorithm's trajectory once the dual variables meet a sufficient lower bound on feasible rewards.

This study investigates offline handwritten mathematical symbol recognition. We outline a methodology that outperforms traditional symbol recognition methods by employing deep learning. The proposed approach replaces conventional techniques, such as contour extraction and hidden Markov models, with autoencoders for segmentation and a softmax classifier for recognition. We investigate a novel application of superconformal quantum mechanics, focusing on a supersymmetry generator that squares to cohomology. Actor-critic reinforcement learning has become a foundational component of many leading RL algorithms. HMC-MAC learns an energy function from observed RL interactions to sample state-action pairs from their joint distribution, thereby reducing the sample size required for evaluating policy gradients. Experimental results on both discrete and continuous environments confirm that our method significantly outperforms existing actor-critic baselines, offering more stable and efficient reinforcement learning.

Although sonar has been employed across various automotive and robotic domains, its adoption for layered navigation remains limited. The system architecture combines multiple downstream methods, including a revised fused sonar perception layer employing a minimum statistical distance criterion, a planned path strategy utilizing minimum statistical distance, and a minimum statistical distance-based control approach. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's reliability, achieving high success rates in both path planning and control.
